## Abstract

The Green Belt is probably England’s most popular and longstanding planning policy commanding widespread political support locally and nationally yet it is regularly critiqued as one of the main causes of England’s Housing Crisis by academics, think tanks and housebuilders. More broadly, following Hall’s seminal work The Containment of Urban England (1973), it is often argued that it contributes to wider inequitable outcomes in the planning system, which is disproportionately skewed in favour of campaigners and homeowners. This thesis critically evaluates the extent to which the Green Belt contributes to the housing crisis and whether the policy needs reforming. The broader question of power in planning is addressed through exploring why and how the public and campaigners support the Green Belt and oppose housebuilding generally. It therefore aims to add nuance to, and move forward the often polarised Green Belt debate by focusing principally on the views of planners, which are often under-represented in the Green Belt debate, despite being the main actor in the planning system. The study focuses on the importance of space through a geographically based case study of the West Midlands.

The thesis finds that the housing crisis is a complex, multi-faceted problem consisting of multi scalar factors although the Green Belt exacerbates the crisis in particular locations, especially on the edge of conurbations. It argues that the policy should not be abolished but modified for the 21 st century with a focus on sustainability, especially recreation and environmental improvement, and that there should be national conversation on the policy’s overall spatial extent and purpose, perhaps as part of a national plan. The study also finds that people primarily support the policy because of popular planning principles and place attachment rather than house prices. There is a gap between the attempted exercises of power and effective power of campaigners with significant circumscription and modulation of power in the planning system. Finally, many of the issues associated with the Green Belt and community opposition to development generally are related to the lack of strategic planning in the current system so the thesis underlines the need for integrated, strategic planning to protect the environment and meet housing need.

## Acknowledgements

After 8 and a half years at the University of Birmingham, it is difficult to know where to start! Firstly, many thanks to my amazing supervisors Mike Beazley and Austin Barber. Thank you Austin for first inspiring me about planning with your amazing lecture on the ‘The Rise of the Entrepreneurial City’ in the Second Year Geography module Urban and Regional Economy! Although I really enjoyed Human Geography at A-Level, I was going to study Single Honours History at Birmingham but then changed my mind to do Joint Honours History with Geography – it has been one of the most important decisions in my life. However, in my first and second year of University, I was more interested in Physical Geography but through your enthusiasm, Austin, you reignited my interest and passion for cities and planning which has continued and deepened since – I am deeply grateful. Fascinated by the effect that planning can have on cities, I attended an Urban Morphology seminar in early 2014 with Dave Adams on the post-war reconstruction of Coventry. This began a friendship which has continued with Dave. Mike, I think that I first properly got to know you at the internal Planning Masters Postgraduate Open Day in 2014 and then at an RTPI Seminar on Arthur Skeffington and community involvement in planning in July 2014! Over that summer I did a lot of reading on planning and economic development, wrote a Report on the growth of cities funded by Careers Network, and began to get more involved in the RTPI. You then very kindly let me onto third year planning modules, Mike and Austin, even though I was not a planning student and this convinced me to undertake a Planning Masters here at Birmingham! Through the Planning Masters, the ESRC-funded Research Masters and three and a half years of the PhD, you have both been a tremendous source of encouragement, help and inspiration despite being so busy with teaching. I have had the privilege of an extended and successful working relationship with you both. You are rightly held in the highest esteem by all and are legends in the planning world as always seeking to make time for people! I will greatly miss our supervision meetings but I am really looking forwards to teaching here at Birmingham and I hope that, now I have finished the PhD, you have a more peaceful retirement Mike!

Before acknowledging the team at CURS and the Geography Department, thanks are due to Professor Richard Cust of the School of History who developed my interest and passion in the English Civil War and, more importantly, encouraged me to become an academic. I greatly enjoyed being your research assistant in the Summer 2015 and apologies for not becoming a Civil War historian but at least I am still an academic! The School of Geography, particularly the CURS team, has been a fantastic support and, to name a few of many, past and present, who have been a great help include Dave Adams and Kat Salter (brilliant and supportive planning colleagues), Lauren Andres (who inspired me during the Planning Masters, encouraged me to research urban farming in Bristol in the Research Masters and who I have continued to work with), Lloyd Jenkins (who steered me through undergraduate and the Research Masters), Rosie Day (PGR lead), Pat Noxolo (PGR lead for Human Geography), Eric Chu (formerly my academic mentor), Joanna Southworth (my undergraduate Personal Tutor who first suggested an academic career), Jon Oldfield (who unfailingly managed to procure planning books for the Library!) and Professor Jeremy Whitehand, who sadly died in June 2021, alongside the wider Urban Morphology Research Group (I miss the Group’s extended lunches in Staff House and the interesting seminars). Professor Whitehand was a tremendous support and help throughout my studies/the PhD and I miss him hugely. The DR Community at Birmingham has been an incredible support. Phil Emerson and Katie Olivers – the original pillars of 225 (our PhD office) – many thanks for helping me to settle into the PhD and then supporting me through it. We

The Green Belt, Housing Crisis and Planning System miss you tremendously at Birmingham. To my longstanding colleagues, Stuart Bowles and Shivani Singh, I had the privilege of beginning the PhD process with you in September 2016 and I have really valued your friendship since. Faye Shortland – I met you a year later in September 2017 and you too have been a tremendous support and help through the PhD, especially encouraging me during the final editing! Congratulations on completing your PhD before me! Caz Russell, Amy Walker, George Willis, Rob Booth, Jessy Shellcross, Polly Jarman, Yanhui Shi and others – I have missed you hugely in 225 since lockdown began nearly a year ago. You have tolerated my interest in the weather, planning, the RTPI, Worcester and the railways incredibly well and with good humour! Lucy Capewell – it has been a pleasure to have started the PhD at the same time as you and I always really enjoy our conversations about hydrology, the weather and CPRE amongst other things. Last but not least, many thanks Gretchel Coldicott for your unfailing support as the PGR Administrator. My sincere apologies if I have missed anyone out in the Department.

In the wider University, I would like to thank the University Graduate School, especially Eren Bilgen, Gavin Schaffer, Georgina Hardy, Nazia Akhtar, Leliana Jardim, Andrea Patel and Katie Hoare, for all your help and support over the years and the wonderful privilege of being Westmere Scholar during 2017/18. Ashleigh Skelhorn, the ESRC Administrator for most of my PhD, you have been a brilliant and helpful Administrator and many thanks for your help with the Researcher Training Support Grant which has enabled me to attend so many interesting RTPI Conferences. I would like to acknowledge the ESRC Studentship which has funded this research and for the training and development opportunities which I have been able to make the most of. Jayne Sharples, Postgraduate Careers Consultant, it has been an absolute privilege to be the longstanding Postgraduate E-Learning Assistant for Careers Network and I have really enjoyed the experience, especially working in such a good team, including Sonia Kumari, Dashi Alpion and Ellen O’Brien. Holly Prescott, PGR Careers Advisor, you have also been a tremendous source of Careers Advice. Professor Bob Scapens – many thanks for the excellent module on Case Study Design and for your guiding influence over the research despite not being a planner!

Of course, thanks goes to the many friends, colleagues and acquaintances in planning academia but particular thanks to Quintin Bradley who has read drafts of my research – I have enjoyed our discussions on the Green Belt even if we do not always agree! Many thanks to Andy Inch who has been a critical friend and really helpful in developing my ideas. You also organised the brilliant collaboration of 22 planning academics to write the ‘Right Answers’ Report – I was delighted to be part of this. There are too many people to name in the planning practice but particular thanks goes to the RTPI. Firstly, the Branch Coordinators, Ella Sumner (West Midlands), Charlotte Daborn (South West) and Susan Millington (South East), many thanks for the free RTPI Conference places in exchange for writing a Report. This has helped me enormously in terms of breaking up the thesis writing, keeping up to speed with developments in planning, making planning connections and given me an excuse to travel the country, especially the beautiful South West! I have really missed face-to face Conferences in the past year and hope that they return as soon as possible when it is safe. I have also really appreciated the way that my research summaries have been published in the Branch Magazines. Aude Bicquelet-Lock, Deputy Head of Policy and Research at the RTPI and an expert in Research Methods, many thanks for your interest in the research, especially for reading a draft of the Methodology! Richard Blyth of the RTPI and Tom Kenny, who was at the RTPI for most of my PhD, many thanks for your interest in the work. To the 73 interviewees, those who took part in the focus groups and responded to the questionnaire, a massive thank you.
